candidates.name: travel-advisory-archive
candidates.what_it_holds: Daily automated archive of US State Dept travel advisories for all 222 tracked countries, split into 4 risk levels (Level 1 Normal Precautions: 87 countries, Level 2 Increased Caution: 83, Level 3 Reconsider Travel: 30, Level 4 Do Not Travel: 22 as of the 2026-09-13 snapshot). Data stored as per-country markdown files under /advisories plus a /data directory; GitHub Actions workflow updates daily. 290 commits, so likely has meaningful history of level changes if commit history is walked (git log on /data gives a point-in-time series of level changes per country). No stars/forks; unclear license.
candidates.why_useful: Advisory-level upgrades/downgrades by country are a direct, point-in-time demand-shock series for regional travel demand (APAC/LatAm/EMEA nights) -- addresses gap #11 (events/shocks) and is a genuinely new asset class we do not currently hold (we only have a 32-factor STR regulatory event database, no travel-advisory series). Because it's git-committed daily, the commit history itself functions as a vintage register (point-in-time levels by date) if it can be walked.
candidates.time_coverage: daily snapshots, exact start date unconfirmed from the fetch (repo has 290 commits; likely started within the last 1-2 years given no-stars/small-repo profile) through 2026-09-13 (still updating)

candidates.name: US_State_Department_Travel_Advisories
candidates.what_it_holds: Daily-updated (12:00 UTC) archive of the US State Dept RSS advisory feed (travel.state.gov/_res/rss/TAsTWs.xml), committed as USSD_TAS.csv (3.73 MB, too large to preview inline -- substantial history) plus ISO_codes.csv for country/region mapping, a travel_map.svg visualization, and feed_test.py (the collection script, reusable as a one-command pull method). BSD-3-Clause licensed. Last commit 2026-08-25.
candidates.why_useful: Same demand-shock rationale as the travel-advisory-archive repo above (advisory-level changes as regional travel-demand shocks, gap #11) but delivered as a single flat CSV (easier to ingest than per-country markdown files) with an explicit, reusable acquisition script and a permissive license.
candidates.time_coverage: daily since an unconfirmed start date through 2026-08-25 (CSV is 3.73MB, implying a multi-year daily archive)
candidates.geography: global, all countries covered by the State Dept feed

candidates.name: fcdo-travel-advice
candidates.what_it_holds: Client/scraper for the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) travel advice API -- a non-Airbnb-site source for a second country's official travel-advisory levels, complementing the US State Dept series. Updated 2026-09-14 (same day as this scout), so actively maintained.
candidates.why_useful: A UK-government advisory series lets a demand-shock construction be cross-checked against a second sovereign source (useful for EMEA-heavy Airbnb markets where UK outbound travelers matter), and diversifies beyond single-source risk in the US State Dept feed.
candidates.time_coverage: current/ongoing pull, no stated historical depth
candidates.geography: global (countries covered by FCDO advice), UK-outbound perspective

candidates.name: fcdo-travel-map
candidates.what_it_holds: A visualization/map front-end over FCDO travel advice data ('a map of all FCDO travel advice'), updated 2026-09-13. Likely pulls the same underlying FCDO source as the repo above but may have its own data snapshot committed.
candidates.why_useful: Second, independently-built FCDO client; worth checking for a committed data snapshot if the gavinmorrison repo's method needs cross-validation.

candidates.name: travel-advice-world-map
candidates.what_it_holds: Interactive world map of Australian Government (Smartraveller) travel advice levels and visa requirements for Australian passport holders. Updated 2026-09-13 (unofficial project pulling the Smartraveller source).
candidates.why_useful: A third sovereign advisory source (Australia) -- useful for APAC-outbound demand-shock cross-checks and diversifying single-country advisory risk; also carries visa-requirement data, a separate friction variable on cross-border travel not covered by any of our current holdings.
candidates.geography: global via Australian Smartraveller, APAC-outbound angle

candidates.name: global_peace
candidates.what_it_holds: Global Peace Index dataset (country-level peace/safety scores) plus Python data-viz files. 2 stars, last updated 2026-02-26.
candidates.why_useful: A slower-moving, annual country-level safety/risk index that could serve as a control variable or cross-check against the higher-frequency advisory-level series above when assessing regional demand risk (e.g., LatAm/APAC safety perception shifts).
candidates.time_coverage: unconfirmed, Global Peace Index is normally annual, methodology dates back to 2007 in the source series

candidates.name: fbi
candidates.what_it_holds: A client library for the FBI's Crime Data Explorer API, exposing UCR (Uniform Crime Reporting) and NIBRS (National Incident-Based Reporting System) crime data by agency/city/state. Last updated 2024-03-11.
candidates.why_useful: A one-command pull method for US city-level crime statistics, which is one of this theme's three named data types (crime by city). Crime trends by city could be tested as a local demand-shock proxy for STR bookings in specific US metros (Austin, New Orleans, Chicago -- all in our 13-city panel).
candidates.time_coverage: pulls whatever history the FBI Crime Data Explorer API exposes (UCR historically back to 1960 at state level, NIBRS more recent and more granular by agency)
candidates.size_hint: small client library, no committed data

candidates.name: fbi-crime-mcp-server
candidates.what_it_holds: An MCP server wrapping the FBI Crime Data Explorer API -- UCR crime estimates, NIBRS incident breakdowns, hate crimes, arrests, human trafficking stats. 1 star, updated 2026-08-21 (actively maintained, most recent of the FBI-API clients found).
candidates.why_useful: Same underlying source as the Pirshtuk/fbi client (US city/agency-level crime data) but more recently maintained and packaged as an MCP tool, which could be plugged directly into an agent pipeline for pulling city crime series without writing scraper code.
candidates.time_coverage: whatever the FBI Crime Data Explorer API exposes
candidates.size_hint: small, no committed data (live API wrapper)
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: same underlying FBI CDE API as Pirshtuk/fbi

candidates.name: data-analysis-tools-bureau-of-justice-statistics
candidates.what_it_holds: An independent third-party profile/catalog of the Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS) public API surface and its data-analysis tools, maintained by 'API Evangelist' as part of a broader series cataloguing US government APIs. Updated 2026-09-12 (very recent). Points to the BJS API itself rather than committing data.
candidates.why_useful: BJS runs the National Crime Victimization Survey and other crime/safety series with different (survey-based, victimization-rate) methodology than FBI UCR/NIBRS -- a useful complement if crime-as-demand-shock work needs a victimization-rate cross-check by region.
candidates.time_coverage: points to BJS's own historical API coverage, not itself a dataset

candidates.name: travel-insurance-claims-analysis
candidates.what_it_holds: Commits travel_insurance.csv, the well-known Kaggle 'Travel Insurance' dataset from a Singapore-based third-party travel insurance servicer: >63,000 records, 11 columns (Claim Status, Agency, Agency Type, Distribution Channel, Product Name, Duration, Destination, Net Sales, Commission, Gender, Age). Cross-sectional (not a time series with dates), and the analysis flags serious data-quality problems (ages 0-118, ~44K missing gender, negative sales/duration, >35K zero-commission rows). Updated 2025-11-07.
candidates.why_useful: This is the single, widely-recirculated Kaggle travel-insurance dataset -- at least 6 near-identical repos on GitHub reanalyze it (KushalS25, adibhattar95, mek9wm, Ivan-R-Septian, S-CHAN11 all found via the same gh search). It is cross-sectional with no dates, so it cannot support the RNPL/cancellation-rate time-series work in gap #3; flagging once for completeness, not as a genuine new find.
candidates.time_coverage: cross-sectional snapshot, no date field confirmed
candidates.geography: Singapore-based agency, destinations global (categorical field, not geocoded)
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: one of >=6 near-identical repos reanalyzing the same Kaggle 'Travel Insurance' CSV; do not re-flag the others (KushalS25/CART-RANDOM-FOREST-ANN-CLASSIFIERS, adibhattar95/Fraud-Claim-Detection-in-Travel-Insurance, mek9wm/travel-insurance_decision-tree_random-forest, Ivan-R-Septian/Travel-Insurance-Claim-Prediction-and-Risk-Optimization, S-CHAN11/Insurance-Claim-Prediction)

notes: WebSearch was already at its 200/200 session budget cap before this scout's first call (shared across all scouts running concurrently) -- all three WebSearch queries returned zero results with an explicit budget-exhausted message. DuckDuckGo (both html.duckduckgo.com and lite.duckduckgo.com) was completely unreachable from this environment (ECONNREFUSED at the network level, not a block page) -- worth flagging to the run coordinator since other scouts relying on DDG as the WebSearch fallback will hit the same wall. Bing's raw HTML search results page is JS-rendered and WebFetch's markdown conversion only sees generic nav chrome (github.com/login, github.blog, etc.), so Bing was a dead end for site:github.com style queries. GitHub's own web search UI (github.com/search?q=...) rate-limited to HTTP 429 (Retry-After 3600) after two calls. The one channel that worked well was the unauthenticated GitHub REST search API via WebFetch (api.github.com/search/repositories?q=...), which returned clean structured JSON (parsed by WebFetch's summarizer) for about 10 queries before it too started 403'ing (likely the ~10 req/min unauthenticated rate limit) -- future scouts in this modality should lead with api.github.com/search/repositories rather than gh search repos (saves the 4-call gh budget) or html search-engine scraping, and should pace queries a few seconds apart to avoid the rate limit. No dedicated 'crime by city' committed dataset (as opposed to an API client) turned up -- all crime hits were either single-city Kaggle re-analyses (SF, Denver, Chicago) or FBI/BJS API clients with no committed data; a scout with more search budget should try Socrata/data.world mirrors of NIBRS/UCR bulk files, and try 'CAP index' or 'insurance-linked securities' + 'ILS' phrasing for the catastrophe/hurricane-insurance angle, which returned nothing here. Also worth another pass: 'Fatality Analysis Reporting System' or 'CDC WISQARS' as adjacent US federal safety series, and OSAC (Overseas Security Advisory Council) country crime & safety reports, which 403'd before I could search it.
